A simple approach to the Landau-Zener formula

Amar C Vutha Affiliation: Department of Physics, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06520, USA Email: amar.vutha@yale.edu
Abstract

The Landau-Zener formula provides the probability of non-adiabatic transitions occuring when two energy levels are swept through an avoided crossing. The formula is derived here in a simple calculation that emphasizes the physics responsible for non-adiabatic population transfer.

pacs
03.65.Ca, 31.50.Gh

Energy level crossings have been of continued interest in physics, beginning with early analyses of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation [1] upto present day applications to the production of ultracold molecules [2] and the understanding of quantum phase transitions [3]. The probability of non-adiabatic population transfer during passage through an avoided level crossing is given by the well-known Landau-Zener formula (LZF) [4]. The usual derivations of the LZF involve the use of mathematical techniques such as contour integrals [4, 5] or Weber functions [1], which might present a barrier to introducing non-adiabatic transitions in a basic quantum mechanics course. However the LZF can be understood using simple undergraduate-level physics, without getting mired in complicated mathematics. In the hope that it may be pedagogically useful and provide some physical insight into non-adiabatic population transfer, here is an elementary derivation of the LZF.

Let |0⟩|0\rangle and |1⟩|1\rangle be two basis states of a system. The state vector is |ψ⟩=ψ0​|0⟩+ψ1​|1⟩|\psi\rangle=\psi_{0}|0\rangle+\psi_{1}|1\rangle. Assume that, at the initial time t=tit=t_{i}, the system is prepared in the |0⟩|0\rangle state: ψ0​(ti)=1,ψ1​(ti)=0\psi_{0}(t_{i})=1,\psi_{1}(t_{i})=0. Let the excited state |1⟩|1\rangle be higher in energy compared to |0⟩|0\rangle by an amount ω0\omega_{0} (we set ℏ=1\hbar=1 everywhere for simplicity). Let these two states be coupled by a general time-dependent interaction. In the rotating wave approximation, the Hamiltonian for this two state system can be written as

H=(0Ω†​e+i​ω​tΩ​e−i​ω​tω0).H=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\Omega^{\dagger}e^{+i\omega t}\\ \Omega\ e^{-i\omega t}&\omega_{0}\end{array}\right). (1)

Here Ω\Omega is the strength of the time-dependent interaction, and ω\omega its frequency.

Following Zener [1], consider a process where the detuning Δ=ω−ω0\Delta=\omega-\omega_{0} is varied linearly with time: dd​t​Δ​(t)≡Δ˙=constant\frac{d}{dt}\Delta(t)\equiv\dot{\Delta}=\mathrm{constant}. This can be accomplished by varying the frequency ω\omega of the perturbation Ω​e−i​ω​t\Omega\ e^{-i\omega t}, or by tuning the energy level splitting ω0\omega_{0} (using a magnetic field, for example). For a constant detuning Δ\Delta, the dynamics of the system can be completely described by the usual Rabi flopping formula for a 2-state system [6], but the Rabi formula is not a solution of the Schrodinger equation when the parameters ω0,ω\omega_{0},\omega are themselves functions of time. The exact analytic solution when Δ\Delta is linearly ramped in time involves Weber functions [1]. However, we shall find that the physics of this process can be understood without recourse to the mathematics of special functions.

The main simplification arises because a time-varying detuning leads to rapid dephasing of coherent Rabi oscillations. Say we model the linear ramp as follows: ω\omega varies discretely in very small steps, each of which lasts for some small duration δ​t\delta t. Within each of these time segments of duration δ​t\delta t the detuning is a constant and the coherent evolution of the system is described by the usual Rabi flopping amplitudes. To obtain the state vector of the system for longer durations, the amplitudes from consecutive time-segments have to be added together. However the different detunings, and therefore different Rabi frequencies, in each segment mean that these amplitudes get added together with lots of different phases. Due to this dephasing introduced by the detuning ramp, the population dynamics of the system can be described quite well by summing the transition probabilities per unit time instead of the amplitudes. We estimate the dephasing time τD\tau_{D} as the duration to accumulate a phase difference of ∼2​π\sim 2\pi rad between Rabi oscillations in consecutive segments: τD∼4​πΔ˙\tau_{D}\sim\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{\dot{\Delta}}}. We will find that exact knowledge of this dephasing time is not necessary to get to the LZF.

Under the action of the time-dependent Hamiltonian HH, the probability per unit time for excitation out of the |0⟩|0\rangle state is the transition rate Γ\Gamma, given by the familiar expression [6]

Γ=Ω2​γΔ2+γ2/4.\Gamma=\Omega^{2}\frac{\gamma}{\Delta^{2}+\gamma^{2}/4}. (2)

Here γ\gamma is the decay rate of the Rabi oscillations, which we set equal to the inverse dephasing time: γ=1/τD∼Δ˙4​π\gamma=1/\tau_{D}\sim\sqrt{\frac{\dot{\Delta}}{4\pi}}.

Let P0​(t)P_{0}(t) be the probability of being in the |0⟩|0\rangle state at a time tt. After a time-segment of duration δ​t\delta t, the probability P0​(t+δ​t)P_{0}(t+\delta t) of remaining in the |0⟩|0\rangle state at the end depends on the transition rate Γ⁡(t)\Gamma(t) within that segment. We have

P0​(t+δ​t)=[1−Γ⁡(t)​δ​t]​P0​(t)≈e−Γ⁡(t)​δ​t​P0​(t).P_{0}(t+\delta t)=[1-\Gamma(t)\ \delta t]\ P_{0}(t)\approx e^{-\Gamma(t)\ \delta t}P_{0}(t). (3)

Therefore the probability P0​(tf)P_{0}(t_{f}) of remaining in |0⟩|0\rangle over the entire duration of the process, from an initial time tit_{i} to a final time tft_{f}, is

P0​(tf)\displaystyle P_{0}(t_{f}) =\displaystyle= exp(−∫titfΓ(t)dt)\displaystyle\exp\Big(-\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}}\Gamma(t)\ dt\Big) (4)
=\displaystyle= exp(−Ω2∫titfγΔ​(t)2+γ2/4dt)\displaystyle\exp\Bigg(-\Omega^{2}\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}}\frac{\gamma}{\Delta(t)^{2}+\gamma^{2}/4}\ dt\Bigg)
=\displaystyle= exp(−2​Ω2Δ˙∫Δ⁡(ti)Δ⁡(tf)γ/2Δ2+(γ/2)2dΔ)\displaystyle\exp\Bigg(-\frac{2\Omega^{2}}{\dot{\Delta}}\int_{\Delta(t_{i})}^{\Delta(t_{f})}\frac{\gamma/2}{\Delta^{2}+(\gamma/2)^{2}}\ d\Delta\Bigg)
=\displaystyle= exp⁡{−2​Ω2Δ˙​[atan⁡(Δ⁡(tf)γ/2)−atan⁡(Δ⁡(ti)γ/2)]}.\displaystyle\exp\Big\{-\frac{2\Omega^{2}}{\dot{\Delta}}\Big[\mathrm{atan}\Big(\frac{\Delta(t_{f})}{\gamma/2}\Big)-\mathrm{atan}\Big(\frac{\Delta(t_{i})}{\gamma/2}\Big)\Big]\Big\}.

The mathematical limits Δ⁡(ti)≪γ/2≪Δ⁡(tf)\Delta(t_{i})\ll\gamma/2\ll\Delta(t_{f}) correspond to the physical case where the detuning is ramped from far below resonance, through the level crossing at Δ=0\Delta=0, ending up far above resonance. In this limit, Equation (4) reduces to the LZF: P0(tf)=exp(−2πΩ2/Δ˙)P_{0}(t_{f})=\exp(-2\pi\Omega^{2}/\dot{\Delta}). In principle, population transfer from |1⟩|1\rangle to |0⟩|0\rangle at a rate given by equation (2) must also be considered. It can be neglected in practice because: (a) with the assumed initial conditions, no considerable population is accumulated in |1⟩|1\rangle until after the resonance is crossed (see figure 2), and (b) from that point on, the detuning from resonance only continues to increase, making the population transfer back into |0⟩|0\rangle increasingly improbable.

Note that the population in |0⟩|0\rangle is completely transferred over to |1⟩|1\rangle for an infinitesimally slow ramp through resonance (Δ˙→0⇒P0​(tf)→0\dot{\Delta}\to 0\Rightarrow P_{0}(t_{f})\to 0). This is an example of adiabatic passage [6]. For any nonzero ramp speed, the probability of a non-adiabatic transition is given by the Landau-Zener formula.
